mainEntity.name: Why does my bottom denture keep falling out when I eat?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lower jaw provides a much smaller ridge for the denture to grip onto compared with the upper jaw, and the tongue and cheek muscles generate forces that can dislodge it during chewing. Bone resorption over time can further reduce the ridge height, worsening the problem. If your lower denture is consistently loose during meals, it may benefit from a reline or adjustment. A dental professional can assess whether the fit has changed and discuss options that may improve stability, including adhesive use or more advanced solutions such as implant retention.

mainEntity.name: Can denture adhesive fix a loose lower denture permanently?

acceptedAnswer.text: Denture adhesive can provide a temporary improvement in retention and comfort, but it is not a permanent solution for a poorly fitting denture. If your lower denture requires large amounts of adhesive to stay in place, this is often a sign that the denture no longer fits the current shape of your jaw properly. In such cases, a professional assessment is recommended. Your dental team may suggest a reline, a new denture, or other options depending on your individual clinical situation.

mainEntity.name: How often should dentures be checked by a dentist?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is generally recommended that denture wearers attend dental reviews at least once a year, though your dental team may suggest more frequent visits depending on your individual needs. These appointments allow the clinician to check the fit of your dentures, examine the soft tissues of your mouth, and identify any early signs of bone changes or tissue irritation. Regular reviews are particularly important for lower denture wearers, as the lower ridge tends to change shape more quickly.

mainEntity.name: Are implant-retained dentures suitable for everyone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Implant-retained dentures can be an excellent option for patients with persistent lower denture instability, but they are not suitable for everyone. Suitability depends on several factors, including the amount and quality of available jawbone, overall general health, medical history, and individual clinical circumstances. A thorough assessment, often including dental imaging, is needed before a treatment plan can be recommended. Your dental team can discuss whether this option may be appropriate for you during a consultation.

mainEntity.name: Do lower dentures get looser over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is common for lower dentures to become looser over time. This is primarily due to alveolar bone resorption — the gradual shrinkage of the jawbone that occurs after natural teeth are lost. The lower jaw typically experiences more rapid and more significant bone loss than the upper jaw. As the ridge shape changes, the denture base no longer fits as closely, reducing retention. Regular dental reviews allow these changes to be monitored, and relines or new dentures can be arranged to maintain a comfortable fit.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to struggle with a new lower denture at first?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is very common for patients to need an adjustment period when wearing a new lower denture. The muscles of the tongue, cheeks, and floor of the mouth need time to adapt to the new appliance. Speaking and eating may feel slightly different initially. Most patients find that comfort and confidence improve over several weeks as they become accustomed to the denture. If discomfort persists or if sore spots develop, it is important to return to your dental practice for a review, as small adjustments can often make a significant difference.
